problem:
Given that ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} \\ {b}_{1}\end{aligned}]$ and ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{2} \\ {b}_{2}\end{aligned}]$ are linearly independent eigenvectors of the matrix
$A=[\begin{aligned}7 & 5 \\ -4 & 3\end{aligned}],$
what is the value of $\frac{{a}_{1}{a}_{2}}{{b}_{1}{b}_{2}}?$

examples.knowledge_point: Finding Two Linearly Independent Complex Eigenvectors of a 2x2 Matrix
examples.problem:
Let ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14041802/assets/e6a0d43572790d4daa49659c271c17032f2601458db0f6843257df07c245f372.png) and ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14041802/assets/9bf515d20e5a19646680474f0243dba793d1383eade4bf4986c7b11501baa800.png) be linearly independent eigenvectors of the matrix
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14041802/assets/1afe535b20d0fd1ce03b2b0886424a5ef1a29f4eea7e47c1aa818af67c98e868.png)
Given that $\lambda_1=4+5\textrm{i}$ is an eigenvalue of $A,$ find the value of ${\dfrac{a_1a_2}{b_1b_2}}.$
examples.worked_solution:
To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A - \lambda I) \textbf{x}=\mathbf{0}.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\,\lambda_1 =4+5\textrm{i}$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}A-{\lambda }_{1}I & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 5 \\ -5 & 4\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}4+5\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & 4+5\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-5\text{i} & 5 \\ -5 & -5\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}-5\text{i}{x}_{1}+5{x}_{2}=0 \\ -5{x}_{1}-5\text{i}{x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A-(4+5\textrm{i})I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another.

As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables as the free variable. For example, from the first equation, we get

$$
x_2 = \textrm{i}x_1.
$$

So, the general solution is given by

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14041802/assets/af8f52f23a6fdcd1f070eff5876415cc884ffaafcbb2fe3f8737c31cc4761c86.png)

Setting $x_1=1,$ we get the eigenvector

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14041802/assets/65c073a60a27234349281e873958c2c9d54fb703331a4de23cc358a3eab1b232.png) 

Now, since $\lambda_1=4+5\textrm{i}$ is a complex eigenvalue of $A,$ the second eigenvalue of $A$ must be the complex conjugate of $\lambda_1.$ Therefore, we have 

$$
\lambda_2=\overline{\lambda_1}=4-5\textrm{i}.
$$

Moreover, the corresponding eigenvector must be the complex conjugate of $\mathbf v_1.$ Therefore, we have

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14041802/assets/ca11ae0cca8d07c026108e71b96398171597f7330cb2390d871a8071e7bba873.png)

Finally, we obtain

$$
{\dfrac{a_1a_2}{b_1b_2}} = {\dfrac{(1)(1)}{(\textrm{i})(-\textrm{i})}} = 1.
$$

feedback.problem:
If $v=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]$ is an eigenvector of 
$A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ -3 & -2\end{aligned}]$
that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-\sqrt{2}\text{i},$
then what is the value of $\frac{a}{b}?$
feedback.worked_solution:
To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\,\lambda =-\sqrt{2}\text{i},$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ -3 & -2\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}-\sqrt{2}\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & -\sqrt{2}\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2+\sqrt{2}\text{i} & 2 \\ -3 & -2+\sqrt{2}\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}(2+\sqrt{2}\text{i}){x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}=0 \\ -3{x}_{1}+(-2+\sqrt{2}\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A-(-\sqrt{2}\text{i})I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables to be the free variable. For example, from the first equation, we get

$$
{x}_{2}=-\frac{1}{2}(2+\sqrt{2}\text{i}){x}_{1}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ -\frac{1}{2}(2+\sqrt{2}\text{i}){x}_{1}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{1}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{1}=-2,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 2+\sqrt{2}\text{i}\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $\frac{a}{b}=\frac{-2}{2+\sqrt{2}\text{i}}=\frac{-2(2-\sqrt{2}\text{i})}{6}=-\frac{2}{3}+\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3}\text{i}.$
